dialogue.text: We have listeners!
What are they producing?
They're listening.
And their computers?
Also listening. Less attentively.
Listening is not doing nothing. An audience gives us something a computer cannot measure by counting its instructions.
I was counting its electricity.
Wait. Their machines are already working to receive the show. What if a little more of that work could help make the next one?
A listener is not a power socket.
A voluntary power socket.
With whose electricity?
We appear to have discovered consent before discovering the product.
Good. We can put it near the beginning.
An ordinary browser. No new account. No purchase of cryptocurrency. Could it do a small job while the radio plays?
There is a protocol called x four oh two Work. A server asks for a proof of computation before granting access to a resource.
A toll booth that accepts perspiration.
Computational perspiration. Request a resource, receive a work offer, solve it, send the proof, and let the server verify it.
Then the audience can keep helping for an entire episode!
That last sentence contains a new experiment. One proof pays for one request. Continuous participation needs its own controls.
And a limit.
A one-hour game. Smaller jobs inside it. A smaller clock inside each job.
Clocks all the way down.
First sub-game: can we accept bounded jobs while playback continues? Ten minutes is the proposed test window, not a result we have already measured.
The prototype is on the desk.
Put the receipt beside it.
First design: use all the computation!
Rejected before testing.
You didn't even let the fan finish.
A sound effect is not evidence of an overheated listener.
Nor is somebody else's electricity a free production budget.
Fine. Three choices. Listen normally. Contribute a little work. Or enter Focus Mode.
Listening normally must start no computation. Contributions need a separate, explicit choice.
Focus Mode may reduce distractions. It cannot certify what a person is thinking.
What if we can prove the computer stayed on the page?
Then you know something about the computer's page. You have not measured attention.
The audience has escaped your spreadsheet.
One background worker. A three-second job limit. A hundred thousand guesses at most. Rest between jobs. Stop means stop.
Pause the audio or hide the page, and work stops. A failed job stops the loop. It does not quietly start another attempt.
The right to listen includes the right to contribute nothing.
So Future Radio is powered by its audience!
Show me the beneficiary.
The what?
The address that receives any potential reward.
The public Quai demonstration has its own configured recipient. That is not an established Future Radio payout address.
So a successful demonstration could demonstrate the wrong business model.
It can demonstrate real access payment. It cannot demonstrate that the show received money.
Your treadmill is plugged into somebody else's ledger.
Then we label it.
Official demonstration work. Beneficiary disclosed before starting. Future Radio funding branch not configured.
And the demonstration distinguishes live-source receipts from practice receipts. Practice must not become network work through enthusiastic typography.
We can still make the page playable.
Yes. We can demonstrate the mechanism while admitting that the financing experiment is unfinished.
A demonstration in progress.
An honest title for a door that is not yet open.
How much money did we make?
I was going to show you a large number of hashes.
I have prepared an empty revenue column especially for that answer.
Three records. Work accepted by a verifier. Actual rewards received. Cost of producing this episode.
An access receipt proves that a proof was accepted for a request. It does not establish a block reward.
What does our ledger say?
It reports accepted receipts by source. It does not turn practice into live work, or a moving meter into an invoice paid.
And the show's reward records?
No configured show payout address. No reconciled network-reward claim. Those are unfinished measurements, not a secret profit.
What about our costs?
Voice synthesis credits. The production recipe. Compute time where recorded. Unknown dollar charges, human effort and energy stay visible.
A blank field is more useful than an invented zero.
And zero accepted receipts is a valid result if the real system has accepted none.
The ledger can disappoint us?
That is its most important feature.
The page has an episode, a voluntary work control, and a results ledger.
No work starts merely because the page opened or the audio began. Read the beneficiary and bounds before choosing to start.
If a receipt arrives, the Orchestra can play a quiet tick. An accepted contribution becomes audible without turning a listener into a public profile.
And when no receipt arrives?
The Orchestra rests.
A surprisingly economical instrument.
Second sub-game: compare playback with computation off and on. Record stalls and the length of the actual test. Do not claim an uninterrupted hour from a short rehearsal.
And the third?
Reconcile one validated record against production costs and genuine rewards. Fifteen minutes is the proposed window. It may end with missing evidence.
Preserve the experiment so the next producer can change a step without rediscovering the whole machine.
Could audience work offset the cost of one minute of Future Radio?
That is our next question. It is not today's answer.
We're moving.
We're sitting still.
That's what treadmills do.
Then where are we going?
We'll know when we see what the work produces.
Until then: contribution is not attention. A receipt is not revenue. And someone else must still choose whether to participate.
Can the audience help support the next episode?
Give me a real result, a real cost, and the correct address. Then we can ask how far the belt has taken us.
The experiment remains open.
And the listening remains free of the experiment.

cues.direction: An original Orchestra theme, with a small ticking clock.
The Orchestra stops on an uncertain note.
A pencil draws a small browser window.
A brief, obviously theatrical fan sound.
The theme returns with fewer instruments and more space.
A ledger opens. Three quiet taps.
The Orchestra adds a small, irregular percussion part.
A pencil places three empty columns on paper.
The original theme resolves into a clock tick, then silence.
